blocks.text: Change the Partition Without Changing the Number

If you divide one unit into three equal parts and take two, you have two thirds. Now divide each third into four equal parts. The unit contains twelve smaller parts, and your portion contains eight. You have neither added nor removed any quantity: \(\frac{2}{3}=\frac{8}{12}\). The names of the parts change, but the point on the number line stays in the same place.

Equivalence is preserved when you multiply the numerator and denominator by the same nonzero integer. That factor transforms all the parts in the same way. Multiplying only the numerator increases the amount you take; multiplying only the denominator reduces the size of each part. Multiplying both by zero is invalid: it would produce a zero denominator and would no longer represent a number.

You can also verify equivalence using cross products. To decide whether 4/7 and 12/21 represent the same number, compare 4 × 21 with 12 × 7. Both products equal 84. This check is valid because neither denominator is zero. It avoids relying on a rounded decimal that could hide differences.

blocks.prompt: Select all the fractions that represent the same number as −3/5. Keep track of the sign when comparing.

options.reviewFeedback: For the selected fraction, check whether its numerator and denominator have the same scaling factor relative to the reference. Keep the sign as well.
For the selected fraction, first interpret the sign of the quotient. Then check the multiplicative relationship between its two terms and those of the reference fraction.
For the selected fraction, check the sign and the proportion of its terms relative to the reference separately.
For the selected fraction, first locate its sign relative to zero. Equivalence must preserve position as well as size.
For the selected fraction, check how the size of the parts changed and how the number of parts taken changed. Examine both changes together.

feedback.correct: −6/10, 9/−15, and −12/20 are all equal to −3/5. In the second fraction, the only negative sign is in the denominator; the quotient is still negative.
feedback.incorrect: 3/5 reverses the sign and is positive. −3/10 still uses three parts, but each part is half as large, so the value changes. The other three fractions change numerator and denominator by the same factor.

blocks.text: Simplifying a fraction means dividing its numerator and denominator by a common nonzero divisor. For example, \(\frac{30}{42}=\frac{5\times6}{7\times6}=\frac{5}{7}\). The sixes are factors of the entire numerator and the entire denominator. Removing them from both leaves the quantity unchanged. Using the greatest common divisor (GCD) takes you directly to a form with no common factor greater than one.

A fraction in simplest form is easier to compare and calculate with, but an unsimplified fraction can be perfectly correct. 30/42 and 5/7 are the same number. In these activities, simplification is required only when the prompt asks for it. If simplest form is requested, write a positive denominator; the sign may appear in front of the whole fraction or in the numerator.

Two negative signs cancel: −18/−30 is positive and simplifies to 3/5. With exactly one negative sign, the quotient is negative: 18/−30 = −3/5. Zero divided by a nonzero denominator is always zero. The simplest form we will use for zero is 0/1; that does not make expressions such as 0/0 valid.

blocks.prompt: Simplify −42/−66 and enter the numerator and denominator of its simplest form, with a positive denominator.

feedback.correct: The two negative signs yield a positive number. The GCD of 42 and 66 is 6: dividing both by six gives 7/11.
feedback.incorrect: Dividing only one of the terms is not enough. If you write −7/11, you have kept a negative sign that already canceled. 14/22 is equivalent, but it still has the common factor two.

blocks.prompt: Match each fraction to its simplest form. Check for a common factor before choosing.

feedback.correct: 18/24 simplifies by dividing by six to give 3/4; 16/28 by four to give 4/7; and 14/35 by seven to give 2/5.
feedback.incorrect: The same divisor must be applied to the top and bottom. Sharing a written digit does not mean sharing a factor; check each equality by cross-multiplying.

blocks.text: Why does using the GCD leave a fraction in simplest form? Write m = d×r and n = d×s, where d is the positive GCD. If r and s still shared a factor e greater than one, m and n would share d×e. That divisor would be greater than d, contradicting the fact that d was the greatest. Therefore, r and s have no positive common divisor other than one. For a negative fraction, perform this check using the magnitude of the numerator and leave the denominator positive.

blocks.prompt: 72/120 is divided by its GCD, 24, to give 3/5. Which argument guarantees that 3/5 is in simplest form?

options.label: It is in simplest form because its digits are less than ten.
options.reviewFeedback: Your argument relies on the digits being small. Revisit what it actually means to be in simplest form: examine the common divisors of the two terms.

options.label: If 3 and 5 shared an e>1, then 24×e would divide both 72 and 120 and exceed their GCD.
options.reviewFeedback: Check why an additional common divisor of the new terms would produce a common divisor of the original terms. Connect this reasoning to the word "greatest."

options.label: Dividing by any common divisor always leaves a fraction in simplest form.
options.reviewFeedback: Your argument generalizes to every common divisor. Consider whether the new terms might still share another factor after dividing by one.

feedback.correct: An additional common divisor would produce a divisor of 72 and 120 greater than 24. This is the general argument; it does not depend on the terms being small.
feedback.incorrect: Small digits do not guarantee simplest form: 4/6 is not simplified. Dividing 72/120 by twelve gives 6/10, which still shares the factor two.

blocks.text: Cancellation applies to factors in a product. In \(\frac{3+6}{3}\), the three in the numerator is an addend: crossing it out against the denominator and leaving 1 + 6 changes the number. You can add first and obtain 9/3 = 3. You can also divide both addends by three: 3/3 + 6/3 = 1 + 2 = 3. Both methods account for the entire numerator.

Before canceling, ask whether the factor multiplies the entire expression on top and the entire expression on the bottom. If necessary, write out the factorization. This check is more useful than searching for identical digits to cross out. The final verification can be simple: replace the fraction with a familiar division and see whether the value keeps the same magnitude.

blocks.prompt: Someone changes (5+15)/5 into 1+15. Choose the correction that preserves the value.

options.reviewFeedback: Check that division applies to the whole sum and that each transformation preserves the expression's value.

options.label: (5+15)/5 = 15, after removing both fives.
options.reviewFeedback: Your transformation removes parts of the expression. Before crossing anything out, identify whether they are factors of the entire numerator or addends.

options.label: (5+15)/5 = 16, because the first addend was divided.
options.reviewFeedback: Your method divides only one addend. Check how much of the numerator the fraction bar covers and what happens to the rest of it.

feedback.correct: The division applies to the entire numerator: 20/5 = 4. Likewise, 5/5+15/5 = 1+3 = 4.
feedback.incorrect: 15 removes an addend and the denominator; 16 divides only the first addend. Neither preserves division of the entire sum.

blocks.prompt: Complete 5/8 = n/40. The letter n stands for the missing numerator, not a new unit.

feedback.correct: Eight becomes forty when multiplied by five. The numerator must also be multiplied by five: n = 25.
feedback.incorrect: Adding 32 to the numerator mimics the denominator's change without preserving the fraction. Keep the same factor: 5 × 5 and 8 × 5.

blocks.prompt: Write 0/9 in the agreed simplest form, with a positive denominator. Both fields describe a single fraction.

fields.label: Simplest form of zero: positive denominator

feedback.correct: 0/9 equals zero and is written in simplest form as 0/1. A denominator of one lets us identify it with the integer zero.
feedback.incorrect: 0/0 does not represent zero: division by zero is undefined. 0/9 preserves the value, but here the simplest form 0/1 was explicitly requested.

blocks.text: To complete 3/10 = 9/d, the numerator was multiplied by three, so the denominator must also be multiplied by three. If we move toward larger parts, we divide both terms by the same factor. An additive relationship such as "I added six to the top and bottom" does not generally preserve the quotient.

feedback.correct: The first equality multiplies both terms by five: d = 60. The second divides both by six: n = 3.
feedback.incorrect: Adding twenty-eight to the top and bottom would give a denominator of forty, but it would change the value. In the second equality, the numerator must also be divided.

blocks.prompt: Compare 2/7 and 5/10. Did adding three to the numerator and denominator preserve the number?

options.label: Yes: the same number was added to the top and bottom.
options.reviewFeedback: Your argument assumes that adding the same number to both terms preserves the quotient. Test that assumption by examining the multiplicative relationship between the terms.

options.label: No: 2×10 = 20 and 5×7 = 35, which are different.
options.reviewFeedback: Review why these products can test whether fractions are equal. Check each product before concluding.

options.label: Yes: both fractions are less than one.
options.reviewFeedback: Your argument treats belonging to the same interval as proof of equality. Reconsider the difference between lying in the same interval and representing the same number.

feedback.correct: They are not equivalent: 2/7 is less than one half, and 5/10 is one half. Equality requires the same multiplicative factor, not the same addition.
feedback.incorrect: Performing the same written operation on both terms does not guarantee equivalence. Being less than one does not make the fractions equal either.

feedback.correct: A single negative sign produces −63/105. The GCD is 21, and the simplest form is −3/5.
feedback.incorrect: 3/5 loses the sign; −9/15 preserves the value, but it still has the common factor three.

feedback.correct: The GCD of 150 and 84 is 6, giving 25/14. An improper fraction can still be in simplest form.
feedback.incorrect: A fraction in simplest form does not have to be less than one. Dividing only the numerator changes the value.

blocks.prompt: To simplify (8+12)/30, select every valid transformation.

options.reviewFeedback: For the selected method, first check the value of the sum in the numerator and then whether simplification applies the same factor to both terms.
For the selected method, verify the factorization of the entire sum and check which complete factor is being canceled.

options.label: (8+12)/30 = (8+2)/3, crossing out the one in twelve and the zero in thirty.
options.reviewFeedback: For the selected method, distinguish a digit from a factor. Check whether the transformed expression preserves the division of the full sum.
For the selected method, check whether the denominator applies to each addend and whether recombining the parts reconstructs the original expression.

feedback.correct: Adding first, factoring the entire sum, or dividing both addends are all valid methods. In b, (2+3) equals five and the factor five cancels from the complete numerator and denominator.
feedback.incorrect: Crossing out digits does not cancel factors. (8+2)/3 equals 10/3, not 2/3; a digit's position does not justify removing it.

blocks.prompt: Both number lines use the same zero and the same unit. Their marks occupy the same position. Select every way to write that number.

options.reviewFeedback: For the selected representation in fourths, identify the distance between marks and count from the shared zero to the shown point.
For the selected representation in eighths, check how many of those parts are needed to reach the mark on the line.
For the selected representation in eighths, relate the numerator to the number of intervals from zero. Do not copy a count made using a different partition.
For the selected representation in twelfths, check an equivalence that places it on the line without changing the unit or origin.

feedback.correct: 3/4 = 6/8 = 9/12. Refining the partition changes how many parts we count without moving the position.
feedback.incorrect: 3/8 keeps the numerator but makes the parts half as large, so it occupies a different position.
